title: US oil inventory preview: five terms to know before Wednesday's EIA data
body: US oil inventory preview: five terms that explain what traders will be watching US crude stockpiles are expected to have risen last week while fuel inventories fell, a Reuters poll showed. Early industry data, however, points the other way on crude. Here's what's expected, and what the key terms in the weekly reports actually mean. What analysts expect Analysts polled by Reuters expect crude inventories to have risen by close to 2 million barrels in the week to 2 October, roughly in line with the five-year average for the time of year. Gasoline stocks are seen falling by a similar amount and distillate stocks by about 2 million barrels. Refinery utilisation is expected to have slipped slightly from about 92.5% of capacity. The previous week's official data surprised the market. Crude stocks rose by about 900,000 barrels to around 427 million, when analysts had expected a small draw. What the API showed The American Petroleum Institute's figures, released after Tuesday's settlement, pointed in a different direction. According to market sources, the API reported a crude draw of about 2 million barrels, against expectations for a build. Gasoline stocks fell by about 1.4 million barrels, while distillates rose by roughly 460,000 barrels. The API data comes from a voluntary industry survey and often differs from the government's figures. The official Energy Information Administration report is due on Wednesday at 10:30 am ET (14:30 GMT) and is the market's benchmark.

title: Japan media reports: BOJ's Sato, one of two September dissenters, backs gradual rate hikes
body: Sato's remarks soften the picture of a hardening dovish bloc that unsettled the yen after September's split vote. When one of the board's most reluctant members accepts that policy is still accommodative, the hurdle for the next hike looks lower, even if timing remains open. The oil link matters most. As a major crude importer, Japan feels Middle East supply disruption directly through import costs, and a dove citing that pressure suggests energy prices are now shaping the policy debate across the whole board. Her rejection of a pre-set pace leaves room to argue for delay, so the yen's response is likely to depend on whether other board members echo the gradual-but-onward message. --- Earlier: BoJ's Sato supports further rate hikes but avoids specifying timing. USDJPY remains confined. --- The Bank of Japan's newest dove has signalled she is not against hiking, only against hurrying, and Middle East oil is doing much of the persuading.

title: Australia Industry Activity Slumps
body: Australia's Industry Index slumped to -24.2 in September from a revised -1.6 in August, highlighting escalating uncertainty as volatile prices and shifting market conditions weigh on investment, orders, and forward planning. Firms reported increasing difficulty in securing finance, while cost pressures remained elevated amid a second wave of fuel and downstream price increases that reignited inflation concerns. The activity/sales index plunged 28.5 points to -31.0, returning to a state of deep contraction. Employment also slipped back into negative territory at -15.6, wiping out the gains seen in August. New orders dropped 22.4 points to -35.9, reversing earlier improvements, and input volumes weakened to -12.9. Input price growth eased, with the index falling 10.6 points to 56.8, but sales prices rose 13.0 points to 13.6, indicating some improvement in firms' ability to pass on costs. Even so, the spread between input and sales price indices remained wide at 43.2 points, keeping profit margins under pressure despite this partial relief. Capacity utilisation slipped to 77.2%, even as businesses continued to grapple with rising costs, labour shortages, and intense competitive pressures. title: Australia Manufacturing Contraction Eases Sharply

The metals sector faced additional headwinds from softer orders, increased import competition, and regulatory constraints. By contrast, conditions improved downstream. title: US Crude Inventories Fall 2.09 Million Barrels
body: US crude oil inventories fell by 2.09 million barrels in the week ending October 2, following a build of 1.019 million barrels the previous week. Over the past 25 weeks, commercial crude stocks excluding the SPR have declined by more than 38 million barrels, even as total US crude inventories have increased by nearly 13 million barrels since the start of the year. An additional 800,000 barrels were released from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), reducing its holdings to 283 million barrels, close to the generally accepted operational minimum range of 250–300 million barrels. Cushing stocks rose by 866,000 barrels. Gasoline inventories fell by 1.37 million barrels after a 2.991-million-barrel build the week before, while distillate inventories increased by 461,000 barrels, reversing a prior 286,000-barrel draw. US crude oil production edged up to 13.955 million bpd in the week ending September 25, from 13.939 million bpd a week earlier. title: Add a new risk to keep oil near $100: Gulf hurricane joins Houthi strikes and Iran tensions
body: The storm's biggest effect may fall on refined products rather than crude. If Gulf Coast refineries shut ahead of landfall, they stop buying crude, which can briefly weigh on US crude prices even as gasoline and diesel tighten. That would widen crack spreads, the margin between crude and the fuels refined from it, at a time when diesel is already at record highs and Western governments are preparing emergency stock releases. Outside the US, the Houthi attacks and Washington's sharper tone on Iran keep a geopolitical premium in Brent that rising Gulf export volumes have so far failed to erode. For now, the balance of risks favours prices holding around $100 rather than falling back, unless the storm weakens or Middle East tensions ease. --- Oil is being pulled between returning Middle East barrels and a growing list of threats, and this week a Gulf of Mexico hurricane joined the queue.

title: SpaceX seeks $40 billion in debt led by Apollo to fund Nvidia chip order, FT says
body: The deal underlines a theme running through bond markets this week: AI is now a major source of corporate debt supply. Goldman Sachs cited AI-related corporate issuance as one of the forces pushing US Treasury yields higher, and a $30 billion investment-grade offering from a single borrower would add to that competition for investor cash. For Nvidia, a large debt-financed order from a customer committed to using its hardware exclusively supports the demand outlook, although the muted share reaction suggests much of that is already priced in. The bigger question for credit markets is appetite. With Morgan Stanley warning of rising caution among lenders, the pricing and take-up of this deal will be a useful test of how much more AI borrowing investors can absorb. --- SpaceX wants to borrow $40 billion to buy Nvidia chips, a reminder that the AI boom is increasingly being built on debt.

title: Two veteran bond bears turn bullish on long Treasuries as yields top 5%
body: Oil remains the swing factor. Higher diesel and gasoline prices from the Middle East conflict feed directly into inflation expectations, and one strategist quoted by Barron's (may be gated) described oil as a wild card for US rates. That means any long-bond rally is hostage to Gulf supply headlines, much as Goldman Sachs suggested in its note. Strong inflows into long-duration funds during a record losing streak show that real money is willing to buy weakness, which could slow the selloff even if it doesn't reverse it. Against that, a Fed on a tightening path, heavy issuance and AI-related corporate borrowing keep upward pressure on yields, so volatility is likely to stay high. - Long Treasuries are having their worst run on record, which is exactly why two of their longest-standing critics have decided it is time to buy.

title: Goldman Sachs sees five drivers behind US rates selloff, says move may be overdone
body: The oil link is the one to watch. In Goldman's account, the energy shock reaches US Treasuries indirectly, through forced selling in UK and euro-area bonds, which means Gulf supply headlines are now a bond market driver as well as a crude market one. With Brent holding around $100, that pressure is unlikely to ease without a de-escalation or a clear improvement in Middle East flows. Higher Treasury yields also tighten financial conditions for equities, credit and housing, the very adjustment Goldman suggests the market is pushing for. For investors, the bank's call is a conditional one: yields may look attractive, but the catalyst for a rally has to come from energy or growth, not valuation alone. --- Goldman Sachs thinks the Treasury selloff has gone too far, but it is not ready to call the turn until oil or the US data give way.

title: Glamsterdam in plain English: how Ethereum plans to cut out the middlemen in block building

title: Japan real wages rise for eighth straight month, backing case for BOJ hikes
body: The detail that matters most for the Bank of Japan is base pay. Regular wages holding steady near 4% points to durable wage growth rather than a bonus-driven spike, which is the kind of evidence policymakers want before tightening further. That supports the yen and front-end Japanese government bond yields at the margin, even as the headline real wage gain slowed. The risk to the real wage picture comes from prices. With the inflation measure used in the calculation only just above 2%, and Tokyo core inflation accelerating alongside elevated oil costs from the Middle East conflict, any pickup in the deflator would quickly erode real gains. That tension matches the Reuters Tankan earlier today, where service firms said inflation was squeezing household purchasing power despite rising pay. - Japanese workers are still getting ahead of inflation, and steady base pay growth gives the Bank of Japan another reason to keep raising rates.

title: Gasoline Rises for Second Day
body: US gasoline futures climbed above $3.30 per gallon, advancing for a second consecutive session, as a storm in the Gulf of Mexico threatened to disrupt refinery operations. Refineries along the US Gulf Coast account for roughly half of the nation's total refining capacity, which is about 18.2 million barrels per day. At the same time, ongoing attacks in the Middle East kept energy-market risks elevated, even as regional shipments showed some improvement. Fuel markets were further tightened by Russia's continued restrictions on diesel exports and refinery outages, as well as reports that China has suspended some fuel exports scheduled for October. According to the EIA, as of September 25 gasoline inventories were 7% below the five-year average, while refinery utilization stood at 92.5%. The agency also raised its oil price forecasts for 2026 and 2027, pointing to rapidly declining global inventories and heightened supply risks. Separately, the G7's planned release of emergency crude and diesel reserves could offer some limited relief to tight markets. At the same time, ongoing attacks in the Middle East heightened worries over energy flows despite higher regional shipments. Additional pressure came from disruptions to Russia's refining sector, prolonged diesel export restrictions, and reports that China has suspended fuel exports for October, all of which intensified global diesel supply constraints. title: Australian Dollar Halts 3-Day Rally
body: The Australian dollar hovered around the $0.70 mark after a three-session rally, as investors looked ahead to key central bank updates for guidance on the policy outlook. In the United States, the Federal Reserve is set to release minutes from its September meeting and several policymakers are scheduled to speak this week. Following a weaker-than-expected labor market report, futures markets now imply roughly an 80% probability that interest rates will be left unchanged this month. The Aussie also drew some support from broad-based weakness in the US dollar, which recorded its steepest decline against the euro as tensions in European bond markets eased. Domestically, however, sentiment was more subdued. Australian consumer confidence fell for the second consecutive month in October, as higher borrowing costs put further strain on household finances and amplified cost-of-living pressures. Interest rate markets currently assign a 75.7% probability that the Reserve Bank of Australia will keep rates on hold in November, with a 24.3% chance of another hike. Investors will also be closely watching the RBA's meeting minutes next week for additional insight into the central bank's policy stance. title: Philippines Manufacturing Output Growth Picks Up in August
body: Manufacturing production in the Philippines rose by 10.8% year-on-year in August, quickening from an upwardly revised 9.9% increase in July. The strongest boost came from the manufacture of computer, electronic, and optical products, which surged 30.1% (up from 15.8%) and accounted for 57.3% of the overall acceleration in the annual growth rate. Other key contributors were transport equipment (11.5% vs 4.9%), basic metals (27.2% vs 23.9%), rubber and plastic products (15.0% vs 9.9%), electrical equipment (10.9% vs 2.9%), and beverages (4.2% vs 3.6%). In contrast, growth eased in the manufacture of coke and refined petroleum products (24.7% vs 47.6%) and food products (1.3% vs 2.6%). Over the January–August period, manufacturing output was 9.3% higher than in the same period a year earlier. The material has been provided by InstaForex Company - www.instaforex.com

title: Philippines Jobless Rate Falls to 5.3%
body: The unemployment rate in the Philippines declined to 5.3% in August 2026 from a four-year high of 6.0% in July. The number of unemployed persons fell to 2.77 million from 3.14 million, while the employment rate rose to 94.7% from 94.0%, with the number of employed persons increasing to 49.79 million from 49.21 million over the same period. The underemployment rate also eased, slipping to 11.9% from 12.9%, with 5.90 million workers seeking additional hours of work or an additional job. On a year-on-year basis, however, labor market conditions were weaker. The unemployment rate in August 2026 remained above the 3.9% recorded in August 2025, while the employment rate was below the year-earlier 96.1%, and the number of employed persons was down from 50.10 million. The underemployment rate was also higher than the 10.7% recorded a year earlier. The services sector continued to be the largest source of jobs, accounting for 61.7% of total employment, followed by agriculture at 20.9% and industry at 17.3%. Average weekly working hours declined to 39.2 in August from 40.6 in July and 41.0 a year earlier. The material has been provided by InstaForex Company - www.instaforex.com

title: Japan Forex Reserves Fall Further in September
body: Japan's official reserve assets fell by USD 29.1 billion (2.4%) in September 2026, declining to USD 1.178 trillion from USD 1.208 trillion at the end of August, and extending the downturn that followed August's record fall. The September decrease was driven primarily by a reduction in foreign currency reserves, which dropped to USD 976.9 billion from USD 995.0 billion. Within that category, securities declined to USD 821.7 billion from USD 839.6 billion, while deposits with foreign central banks and the Bank for International Settlements eased to USD 154.8 billion from USD 155.0 billion. Gold reserves also decreased, falling to USD 113.6 billion from USD 124.1 billion. Special Drawing Rights (SDR) holdings slipped to USD 60.8 billion, and Japan's reserve position at the IMF edged down to USD 11.3 billion. Other reserve assets were little changed at USD 15.8 billion. The latest decline follows the record USD 79.6 billion drop in August, which came after Japan conducted a ¥15.4 trillion yen-buying intervention to support its currency. title: Japan Nominal Wage Growth Tops 3% for 7th Month
body: Average cash earnings in Japan rose 3.8% year-on-year in August 2026, slightly above market expectations of a 3.7% increase but slower than the revised 4.3% gain recorded in July. This marked the 56th consecutive month of nominal wage growth and the seventh straight month with growth above 3%, the longest such streak since 1992. Regular pay, including base salaries, increased by 3.8%, indicating continued solid wage momentum, while overtime pay accelerated, climbing 5.2% after a revised 4.5% rise in July. In contrast, special payments—mainly one-off bonuses—were flat, following a revised 5.3% jump in the previous month. Wage gains were particularly pronounced in finance and insurance (9.7%), electricity and gas (7.7%), and information and communications (4.8%), whereas wages in living-related services fell 2.1%. Meanwhile, real wages increased 1.5%, extending their run of gains to eight consecutive months—the longest in nearly a decade—though the pace eased from a revised 2.0% rise in July.
